what: Champion Homes builds factory-made houses. It manufactures manufactured and modular homes in plants across North America and sells them through independent dealers, its own retail stores and to community operators and builders.
customers: Buyers of affordable homes across the United States and Canada, plus land-lease community operators and developers buying in volume.
money: Manufactured and modular homes built in plants and sold through dealers and retail.
Mortgage and insurance services for buyers.
moat: Factory construction costs substantially less per square foot than site building, because labour is concentrated, weather is irrelevant and materials are bought in volume. In a country where housing affordability has deteriorated badly and skilled construction labour is scarce, that cost advantage is worth more over time.
risks: Revenue swung from $2.6B in 2023 to $2.0B in 2024, showing how fast demand moves with interest rates.
The shares trade at about 27.1 times earnings and 15.4 times EV/EBITDA, which is a full price for a housing manufacturer.
Buyers of affordable homes are more sensitive to interest rates and credit availability than conventional homebuyers.
Factory capacity is a fixed cost: when orders fall, plants run below capacity and margins compress quickly.
Only six analysts cover the stock, so the $107.00 average target rests on thin coverage.
opportunities: Cash of $638.3M against only $50.8M of debt is an exceptionally strong balance sheet for a housing company.
Revenue has recovered to $2.7B trailing, and last year’s net margin was 7.8%.
Free cash flow of $229.9M on $2.7B of revenue converts well.
Factory-built homes address an affordability problem that keeps getting worse, which is a structural rather than cyclical driver.
Scarce construction labour makes factory production relatively more attractive over time.
watch: Home shipments and average selling price. Volume is the cycle, price per home tells you about mix and whether pricing is holding.
view: The case for factory-built housing is simple and getting stronger: building a house in a controlled factory, with labour concentrated in one place and no weather delays, costs materially less per square foot than building on a site. American housing affordability has deteriorated badly and skilled construction labour is genuinely scarce, so a method that uses less labour and costs less per square foot should gain share over time. That is a structural driver rather than a cyclical one.

What makes Champion attractive relative to its sector is the balance sheet: $638 million of cash against $51 million of debt. Housing manufacturers fail in downturns because they carry inventory and debt into a collapse in orders. Champion has more cash than most competitors have revenue cushion, which means it can keep plants running, keep its dealer network supplied, and buy capacity cheaply when weaker operators struggle. In a cyclical industry, that is worth a great deal.

The cyclicality itself is severe and should not be downplayed. Revenue went from $2.6 billion to $2.0 billion in a single year. Buyers of affordable homes are at the margin of qualifying for credit, so a rise in mortgage rates removes them from the market entirely rather than merely making them choose a smaller house. And factory capacity is a fixed cost — when orders fall, plants run below capacity and margins compress fast.

At 27.1 times earnings and 15.4 times EV/EBITDA, the price assumes the recovery to $2.7 billion continues. That is a growth multiple on a cyclical manufacturer, and the structural case justifies some of it. I would own this for the balance sheet and the affordability thesis rather than for the current multiple, and I would judge it on shipments and average selling price rather than revenue.
bull: Worsening affordability and scarce construction labour push share toward factory building, and a cash-rich manufacturer takes capacity while rivals struggle.
bear: Mortgage rates keep affordable-home buyers from qualifying, plants run below capacity and margins compress, and a 27 times multiple on a cyclical derates.
